summary: Teach probability as a magnitude on a bounded 0-to-1 line, with landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain). The same probability can be written three ways — fraction, decimal and percentage (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) — and children should move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood. Stress the bounds (never below 0 or above 1) and reconnect 0.5 to the informal 'even chance' learned earlier. Comparing mixed notations requires converting to a common form, not ranking by surface digits or by denominator size.
misconceptions: Believing a probability can be greater than 1, or giving a probability as a raw count (e.g. '6' because a die has six outcomes)
Fraction interference — thinking a larger denominator means a larger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
Comparing mixed notations by surface digits without converting (ranking 40%, 1/4, 0.3 as 40 > 4 > 0.3)
Treating 0.5 / 'even chance' as the default for any two-outcome event

activities.title: One position, three notations on a draggable scale
steps: Drag a marker along a 0-to-1 line; a readout shows wherever you land simultaneously as a fraction, a decimal AND a percentage, so 2/5, 0.4 and 40% appear together at the same point.
Place the 'chance of rain 40%' event and watch the marker coincide exactly with 0.4 and 2/5 — confirm these are one position written three ways, not three different chances.
Feed a computed probability from a bag or spinner and watch it snap onto the line at its matching position.
Try to shove the marker past the 'certain' end for a 'probability of 2' and notice it refuses to move beyond 1.
activities.insight: A probability is a single magnitude on a bounded line; the fraction, decimal and percentage are three ways of writing the same position, and nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1).

activities.title: Place, order and match mixed-notation probabilities
steps: Use a slider to place 1/4 and 0.7 on the 0-to-1 line.
Order 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely, converting each to a common form (decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4) before deciding.
Spot and reject an impossible probability, such as a value greater than 1 or below 0, explaining why it cannot be a valid probability.
activities.insight: Comparing probabilities written in different notations requires converting to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line); surface digits and denominator size are not reliable guides, and every valid probability lies between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Landmark reference line with revealed equivalents
steps: Tap each landmark (0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1) to reveal its fraction, decimal and percentage.
At each landmark, read an everyday event that belongs there (e.g. an impossible event at 0, a certain event at 1, an even-chance event at 1/2).
Use the revealed values as a reference while completing placement and ordering tasks.
activities.insight: Each landmark on the scale has a fixed fraction/decimal/percentage identity and a matching kind of everyday event, giving a stable reference for the triple notation.

activities.title: Socratic probing of the bounds
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'the probability is 6' or 'could a probability be 2?' by explaining what 0 and 1 mean.
Locate a claimed value like '6' or '2' on the 0-to-1 line and explain why it cannot sit there.
Describe an event at 0 (impossible) and an event at 1 (certain) in your own words.

Judge a claim like 'any event with two possible outcomes has probability 1/2' — decide whether it is always true, using an example such as a biased spinner or an event much more likely than its alternative.
activities.insight: Nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a raw count of outcomes is not a probability; and 0.5 is the even-chance value only when the two outcomes are equally likely, not automatically for any two-outcome event.

checkQuestion: Show three events with their probabilities written in different notations: Event A has probability 1/4, Event B has probability 0.3, Event C has probability 40%. Ask the child to order them from least to most likely and to place each on a 0-to-1 line. Take the order, then ask them to explain the reason (Tier 2) — how they compared numbers written in different ways.
checkAnswer: Least to most likely: A (1/4 = 0.25), then B (0.3), then C (40% = 0.4). Converting all three to the same form — decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, or positions on the line — shows the order; each sits between 0 and 1, with A a quarter of the way, B just above it, and C below the halfway point.
